citations.quote: For a nonnegative integer $q$, let $M=2^q$, let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ when $M>1$, and let $a=(a_0,\ldots,a_{M-1})\in\mathbb C^M$. The forward discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is the vector $\widehat a\in\mathbb C^M$ with $\widehat a_k=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}a_j\omega^{jk}$. The radix-two procedure returns this vector by the following exact recursion. If $M=1$, return $(a_0)$. If $M>1$, recursively compute the length-$M/2$ DFTs $E$ and $O$ of $(a_0,a_2,\ldots,a_{M-2})$ and $(a_1,a_3,\ldots,a_{M-1})$, using the primitive root $\omega^2$. For $0\le k<M/2$, return $\widehat a_k=E_k+\omega^k O_k$ and $\widehat a_{k+M/2}=E_k-\omega^kO_k$. The inverse transform is obtained by running the same procedure with $\overline\omega$ and dividing every output by $M$.

derivations.claim: For $0\le j,\ell<M$, the $(j,\ell)$ entry of $F^*F$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\omega^{(\ell-j)k}$. If $j=\ell$, this sum is $M$. Otherwise $\omega^{\ell-j}\ne1$ and the finite geometric-sum identity gives $\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\omega^{(\ell-j)k}=(1-\omega^{M(\ell-j)})/(1-\omega^{\ell-j})=0$. Thus $F^*F=MI$, which gives the asserted inverse.

Splitting the DFT sum into even and odd indices gives $E_k+\omega^kO_k$ for $0\le k<M/2$. For frequency $k+M/2$, the even factor is unchanged because $\omega^{jM}=1$, while the odd factor changes sign because $\omega^{M/2}=-1$. Therefore the outputs in [F1] are exactly the defining DFT sums. Induction on $q$, starting with $M=1$, proves exactness of the recursion.

At length $M>1$, forming both half-length transforms and combining their $M$ outputs costs at most $cM$ arithmetic operations for an absolute constant $c$. Hence $T(M)\le2T(M/2)+cM$ and $T(1)=O(1)$; expanding this recurrence for $q=\log_2M$ levels gives $T(M)=O(M\log(2+M))$. The input, output, and one level of butterflies require $O(M)$ workspace; the inverse has the same cost plus coordinatewise scaling by $1/M$.

Let $f,g$ have degree less than $n$, and choose $M'=2^{\lceil\log_2(2n-1)\rceil}$. Pad their coefficient lists to length $M'$, apply the forward DFT, multiply corresponding transformed coordinates, and apply the inverse DFT. For coefficient index $s$, the inverse-transform formula expands it as $\sum_{j,\ell} f_jg_\ell\,M'^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{M'-1}\omega^{(j+\ell-s)k}$; step 1.1 makes the inner sum one exactly when $j+\ell\equiv s\pmod {M'}$ and zero otherwise. Thus the result is cyclic convolution modulo $z^{M'}-1$. The ordinary product has degree at most $2n-2<M'$, so no coefficient wraps around and the result is the exact polynomial product. Since $2n-1\le M'<2(2n-1)$ when $n>1$ (and $M'=1$ when $n=1$), step 3.1 gives $O(n\log(2+n))$ operations and $O(n)$ space.

Here $X^*$ denotes conjugate transpose; a square complex matrix $H$ is normal when $H^*H=HH^*$; and a square matrix $V$ is unitary when $V^*V=VV^*=I$. A matrix is in diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=\Lambda-PQ^*,
$$
where $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is diagonal and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. It is in normal-plus-low-rank (NPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=V\Lambda V^*-PQ^*,
$$
where $V\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is unitary, $\Lambda$ is diagonal, and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. The unitary state change $\widetilde x=V^*x$ converts this NPLR representation to DPLR form and changes $B,C$ to $V^*B,V^*C$, respectively.

For a step size $\Delta>0$ such that $I-\Delta A/2$ is invertible, the bilinear recurrent matrices are
$$ \overline A=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}(I+\Delta A/2),\qquad \overline B=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}\Delta B,\qquad \overline C=C. $$
With initial state $x_{-1}=0$, the discrete recurrence is $x_t=\overline A x_{t-1}+\overline B u_t$, $y_t=\overline C^*x_t$. Its length-$L$ impulse kernel is the vector $K_L=(\overline C^*\overline A^j\overline B)_{j=0}^{L-1}$. For a nonzero direct term $D$, the output has the additional separate skip term $Du_t$.

For a filter evaluation of transform length $M\ge L$, the output vector for the length-$M$ truncated generating function is $\widetilde C_M=(I-\overline A^M)^*C$. A filter procedure may receive $\widetilde C_M$ as given data; an operation count for evaluating the filter from this transformed vector does not include the separate work of forming it from $C$.

derivations.claim: Put $w_n=\sqrt{2n+1}$ and define the real skew-symmetric matrix $S$ by $S_{nk}=-w_nw_k/2$ for $n>k$, $S_{nk}=w_nw_k/2$ for $n<k$, and $S_{nn}=0$. The transpose is $-S$, so over $\mathbb C$ its conjugate transpose is also $-S$; hence $S$ is normal. With $v=w/\sqrt2$, entrywise comparison gives $G^S=(S-\tfrac12I)-vv^*$: below the diagonal the entries are $-w_nw_k$, above they cancel to zero, and on the diagonal they are $-\tfrac12-(2n+1)/2=-(n+1)$. Since a scalar shift of a normal matrix is normal and $vv^*$ has rank at most one, this is the required LegS decomposition. This assertion concerns the finite coefficient matrix only; the factor $1/t$ in the LegS ODE remains time-dependent.

Define $S$ with entries $-1/2$ below the diagonal, $+1/2$ above it, and zero on the diagonal. It is real skew-symmetric and therefore normal. For $e=(1,\ldots,1)^T$, entrywise comparison gives $G^L=(S-\tfrac12I)-\tfrac12ee^*$: below the diagonal the two terms sum to $-1$, above they sum to zero, and on the diagonal they sum to $-1$. Thus the original LagT generator is a normal matrix minus a rank-at-most-one matrix.

For LegT let $D=\operatorname{diag}(2n+1)_{n=0}^{N-1}$ and $E=\operatorname{diag}((-1)^n)_{n=0}^{N-1}$. Define $T_{nk}=1$ for $n\ge k$, and $T_{nk}=(-1)^{k-n}$ for $n<k$. Then direct entry evaluation gives $G^T=-DETE/\theta$: for $n\ge k$, $(-1)^n(-1)^k=(-1)^{n-k}$, while for $n<k$, $(-1)^n(-1)^{k-n}(-1)^k=1$. Write $T=S+R$, where $R_{nk}=1$ when $n$ and $k$ have the same parity and is zero otherwise. The matrix $R$ is the sum of the outer products of the even-index and odd-index indicator vectors, so its rank is at most two. For opposite parities, $S_{nk}=1$ below the diagonal and $S_{nk}=-1$ above it; for equal parities and on the diagonal, $S_{nk}=0$. Thus $S^T=-S$. The invertible diagonal matrix $S_0=D^{1/2}E$ gives $S_0^{-1}G^TS_0=-\theta^{-1}D^{1/2}SD^{1/2}-\theta^{-1}D^{1/2}RD^{1/2}$. The first term is real skew-symmetric and hence normal; the second has rank at most two. The diagonal similarity is essential: this proves the claim for an equivalent state-space matrix, not unitary similarity of the raw LegT matrix.

In each case write the resulting generator as $H-UV^*$ with $H$ normal: for LegS and LagT the factors are the displayed real vectors divided by $\sqrt2$, and for LegT use the even and odd indicator columns multiplied by $D^{1/2}/\sqrt\theta$ as both factors. By [F2], choose a unitary matrix $V_0$ with $V_0^*HV_0=\Lambda$ diagonal. Then $V_0^*(H-UV^*)V_0=\Lambda-(V_0^*U)(V_0^*V)^*$, preserving the low-rank bound. If the original coordinates were changed by $S_0$, the total state change is $x=S_0V_0z$; substitution into $x'=Gx+Bu$, $y=C^*x$ gives $z'=(V_0^*S_0^{-1}GS_0V_0)z+V_0^*S_0^{-1}Bu$ and output vector $V_0^*S_0^*C$. These are exactly the state-coordinate transformations required for an equivalent DPLR model.

Input an integer $M=2^q$ with $q\ge0$, a primitive $M$th root of unity $\omega$, a finite list of poles $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in\mathbb C$, and weights $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb C$. The required output is $y_k=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j/(\omega^k-\mu_j)$ for $0\le k<M$, provided no denominator is zero. If $n=0$, return the zero vector.

Here a primitive $M$th root means $\omega^M=1$ and $\omega^k\ne1$ for $1\le k<M$. For $n\ge1$, form a balanced binary tree on the pole indices, splitting each consecutive index interval into two intervals whose sizes differ by at most one. At a leaf containing index $j$, store polynomials $D_j(z)=z-\mu_j$ and $P_j(z)=a_j$. At an internal node with disjoint child index sets $I_1,I_2$, store
$$ D_I(z)=D_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z),\qquad P_I(z)=P_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z)+D_{I_1}(z)P_{I_2}(z). $$
At the root, fold the coefficients of each polynomial modulo $z^M-1$: the coefficient at degree $r$ is replaced by the sum of coefficients at degrees congruent to $r$ modulo $M$. Let $\omega_0=e^{-2\pi i/M}$, which equals $1$ when $M=1$. Apply the radix-two DFT procedure to each folded coefficient vector to evaluate $P_I$ and $D_I$ at $\omega_0^j$, $0\le j<M$. If $M>1$, find the unique odd integer $s\in\{1,3,\ldots,M-1\}$ with $\omega=\omega_0^s$ by generating and comparing the $M$ powers of $\omega_0$, then place the value at index $sk\bmod M$ at output index $k$; this is the supplied root order because $\omega^k=\omega_0^{sk}$. For $M=1$, the only root is $1$ and no reindexing is needed. This root search and reindexing use $O(M)$ operations. If some reindexed $D_I(\omega^k)=0$, return status `collision`; otherwise return $y_k=P_I(\omega^k)/D_I(\omega^k)$.

Let $M=2^q$ for an integer $q\ge0$, and let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ (with $\omega=1$ when $M=1$). Define the forward DFT matrix $F\in\mathbb C^{M\times M}$ by $F_{kj}=\omega^{jk}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. Then $F^*F=MI$, so the inverse DFT is $M^{-1}F^*$. The radix-two procedure defined on this page computes either transform exactly in $O(M\log(2+M))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(M)$ space. Consequently, for every integer $n\ge1$, two polynomials of degree less than $n$ can be multiplied exactly in $O(n\log(2+n))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n)$ space by zero-padding to a radix-two transform length at least $2n-1$.

derivations.claim: For a leaf containing index $j$, $P_j(z)/D_j(z)=a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ whenever $z\ne\mu_j$. If the identity $P_I/D_I=\sum_{j\in I}a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ holds for the two child sets, then the internal-node formulas in [F1] give $P_I/D_I=P_{I_1}/D_{I_1}+P_{I_2}/D_{I_2}$. Induction up the finite tree therefore gives $P_I(z)/D_I(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ at the root wherever its denominator is nonzero.

The balanced tree has height at most $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. At a node whose index set has size $s$, its three polynomial products have operand degrees at most $s$; by [F2] they cost $O(s\log(2+s))$ operations. At a fixed height, the node index sets are disjoint and their sizes sum to at most $n$, so that height costs at most $O(n\log(2+n))$. Summing over the height gives $O(n\log^2(2+n))$ operations, including the coefficient additions. A depth-first evaluation stores at most one completed sibling subtree per level; their coefficient-array sizes form a geometric sum bounded by $O(n)$, so the product-tree workspace is $O(n)$.

Write the root coefficients as $P_I(z)=\sum_j p_jz^j$ and $D_I(z)=\sum_j d_jz^j$. For each $0\le r<M$, fold them to $p'_r=\sum_{j\equiv r\pmod M}p_j$ and $d'_r=\sum_{j\equiv r\pmod M}d_j$. Since $\omega^{kM}=1$, evaluating the folded polynomials at $\omega^k$ gives exactly $P_I(\omega^k)$ and $D_I(\omega^k)$. The algorithm evaluates both folded arrays with two radix-two DFTs on the standard grid $\omega_0^j=e^{-2\pi i j/M}$; if $M>1$, the supplied primitive root is $\omega=\omega_0^s$ for a unique odd $s$, so reindexing the standard outputs at $sk\bmod M$ gives their values at $\omega^k$. For $M=1$ the grids coincide. By [F2] the two transforms cost $O(M\log(2+M))$ operations and $O(M)$ additional space; finding $s$ and reindexing cost $O(M)$ operations and space, within the same bounds. Folding costs $O(n)$ operations and $O(n+M)$ space.

The noncollision hypothesis makes $D_I(\omega^k)=\prod_j(\omega^k-\mu_j)\ne0$ for every $k$. Thus the divisions in [F1] are defined, and step 1.1 identifies each quotient with the required Cauchy sum. Adding the product-tree, folding, transform, and division costs gives $O((n+M)\log^2(2+n+M))$ operations and $O(n+M)$ space.

The root $-1$ is handled directly and is never included in this Cauchy evaluation. Matrix products and inversions of the $r\times r$ corrections are performed separately at each root.

The recurrent solver may exploit the diagonal-plus-low-rank structure as follows. Write $d_j=1-\alpha\lambda_j$, let $J=\{j:d_j\ne0\}$ and $Z=\{j:d_j=0\}$. derivations.claim: If $n=0$, return zero; if $M=1$, sum the $n$ nonzero-denominator fractions directly, using $O(n+1)$ operations and space, and use the rounding argument below. Otherwise construct a binary tree on consecutive root indices. Its root covers all roots, with center $0$ and radius $1$. At depth $\ell\ge1$, a node contains $m=M/2^\ell$ consecutive roots starting at index $b$; its center is $c=\exp(2\pi i(b+(m-1)/2)/M)$ and its covering radius is $R=2\sin(\pi(m-1)/(2M))\le\pi 2^{-\ell}$. These disks contain their roots because the largest angular distance from the arc midpoint is $\pi(m-1)/M$. Singleton leaves have radius zero. For each pole start at the root: at a nonleaf stop at a far node if $|c-\mu_j|\ge3R/2$, or descend into both children if $|c-\mu_j|\le2R$. In the overlap either choice is valid. A singleton is evaluated directly if reached. Certified interval tests terminate: for $R>0$, the two thresholds have a positive gap $R/2$, so enclosures of width less than $R/4$ distinguish at least one admissible choice, even when one threshold is an equality. Squared-distance comparisons implement the same test with a positive gap and finitely accurate supplied coordinates.

At a fixed depth put $J=2^\ell$. The $J$ arc centers are equally spaced on the unit circle and have mutual distance at least $2\sin(\pi/J)\ge4/J$ for $J\ge2$, by concavity of sine on $[0,\pi/2]$. Every near center lies within $2\pi/J$ of its pole. Disks of radius $2/J$ about these centers have disjoint interiors and lie in the disk of radius $(2\pi+2)/J$ about that pole. Comparing their areas bounds the number of near centers by $(\pi+1)^2<18$. Thus there are fewer than $36$ candidate children per pole at the next depth, including all far stops. The root contributes one candidate. The $q+1$ depths therefore contain $O(n\log(2+M))$ pole/node pairs. Each root follows exactly one stopped or singleton node for each pole, so these pairs partition all pole/root interactions without duplication. Repeated poles obey the same argument separately.

For a stopped pair put $t=-(z-c)/(c-\mu_j)$. Its targets satisfy $|t|\le2/3$. The finite geometric identity gives $1/(z-\mu_j)=\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}(-(z-c))^h/(c-\mu_j)^{h+1}+t^p/(z-\mu_j)$. Therefore the error in this pair is at most $(2/3)^p|a_j|/|z-\mu_j|$. Summing the partition from step 2.1 gives error at each root at most $(2/3)^p\sum_j|a_j|/|z-\mu_j|\le(2/3)^p A/d$. Choose $p\ge1$ with $(2/3)^p\le\eta/2$; then $p=O(\log(1/\eta))$ and the truncation error is at most $\eta s/2$. Direct singleton interactions have zero truncation error.

Process depths successively, keeping the bounded near list per pole for the next depth and the bounded far list for the current depth. At a fixed depth, store $v_{j,I}=1/(c_I-\mu_j)$ and initially $w_{j,I}=a_jv_{j,I}$ for each far pair. Initialize one target power $t_k=1$ per root. For degrees $h=0,\ldots,p-1$, clear one coefficient $g_I$ per current-depth node, add every current $w_{j,I}$ to its node's $g_I$, and add $g_{I(k)}t_k$ to each target accumulator, where $I(k)$ is its unique ancestor at this depth. Update $w_{j,I}\leftarrow w_{j,I}v_{j,I}$ and $t_k\leftarrow-(z_k-c_{I(k)})t_k$. A node without stopped pairs has coefficient zero. Discard the depth's arrays before advancing; at leaves add all direct pairs. The sums are exactly the polynomials in step 3.1. Each depth/degree uses $O(n+M)$ operations and words by step 2.1; the near/far lists, current coefficients, powers and output arrays occupy $O(n+M)$ words. No array of $p$ moments and no list across all depths is stored. The binary root tree has fewer than $2M$ nodes, so its supplied constants and routing data also occupy $O(M)$ words. Routing costs $O(n\log(2+M)+M)$ operations; fixed-width certified interval arithmetic for each overlapping test has constant scalar cost at its supplied sufficient precision. Total cost is $O((n+M)\log(2+M)p)$, with $O(n+M)$ words independently of $p$.

Fix the certified routing and the exact truncated rational circuit just constructed. Nonleaf far denominators are nonzero by their distance test; leaf denominators are nonzero by [A1]. Its finite exact intermediates and denominators admit the stated $V,D$. Suppose all already formed operands have error at most $e\le\min(1,D/2)$. Addition or subtraction increases error by at most $2e+u$. Multiplication increases it by at most $(2V+1)e+u$. For division, writing exact operands as $x,y$, approximate operands as $x',y'$, and $|y|\ge D$, gives $|y'|\ge D/2$ and $|x'/y'-x/y|\le2e/D+2Ve/D^2$; the final rounding adds $u$. Conjugation and changing signs do not increase error. All these bounds are at most $Ke+u$ for the stated $K\ge2$. Input constant error is at most $u$. Induction over the $T$ gates bounds every operand error by $2uK^{T+1}$: more precisely after $t$ gates the maximum error is at most $u(1+K+\cdots+K^t)\le2uK^t$. The stated choice of $u$ keeps this within $\min(1,D/2,\tau)$, so every division remains defined and the output rounding error is at most $\tau$. Root and pole approximation errors are included as input errors in this recurrence. The certified routing uses exact admissible inequalities, so rounding cannot route a pair outside its valid geometric estimate; the positive overlapping gap in step 1.1 permits finite enclosures, whose sufficient precision can be selected together with this $u$.

Combine the truncation and rounding errors to obtain $\max_k|\widehat y_k-y_k|\le\eta s$. For absolute error $\delta$ apply the construction with $\eta=\delta/s\le1/2$, obtaining $p=O(\log(s/\delta))$. These substitutions do not change the memory argument. The elementary example $y=1/(z-\mu)$ changes by $h/((z-\mu)(z-\mu-h))$ when $\mu$ changes to $\mu+h$, showing why separation-dependent precision cannot be omitted from an absolute-error statement.
